title: Designing Complex Enterprise Workflows
subtitle: The procurement intake platform: 6 stages, 98+ screens, 12 iterations

slides.title: Designing Complex Enterprise Workflows
slides.standfirst: End-to-end design of a procurement intake platform for specialists managing millions in annual spend — and one architectural bet, defended with evidence, against the easier answer.
slides.notes: Frame the whole talk around the wizard decision. Everything else is craft; that was the judgement call, and it was the one that could have gone wrong.

slides.title: Sold as a platform, worked as a pile of tools
slides.standfirst: Procurement teams manage millions in annual spend across disconnected tools with no single source of truth.

bullets.text: Users dropped what they knew every time they moved between stages.
Scenario comparison was slow and error-prone.
Supplier qualification held up everything downstream.

callout.text: High abandonment at scenario comparison — where a user weighs 3 to 8 suppliers against 10+ evaluation criteria with no unified view of bids, suppliers and criteria.

figure.alt: The fragmented set of tools procurement specialists were working across

slides.notes: Abandonment at a specific stage is the gift here. It turns a vague complaint into a place to point a research budget.

slides.title: A wizard would have been easier to design, build, test — and wrong
slides.standfirst: Linear flows encode an assumption: that the work is sequential. The research showed procurement is not. Specialists jump constantly between bids, scenarios and supplier data.

bullets.text: Section-based structure with persistent stepper navigation.
Significantly reduced back-and-forth in daily use.

callout.text: Card sorting and task-flow testing, before commitment — then defended with that evidence to three engineering teams and a stakeholder group across product, engineering and procurement.

slides.notes: Be honest that the trade-off is real. A worse first run in exchange for a better thousandth run is defensible only if you can say which one you optimised for and why.

slides.title: Sections you can enter from anywhere, with a stepper that never leaves

figure.caption: Flexible access, with orientation always on screen

slides.notes: The stepper is what makes non-linear tolerable. Freedom without a position indicator is just being lost.

slides.title: Progressive disclosure: scan the category, open the supplier
slides.standfirst: Category summary cards for fast scanning; expandable rows revealing full supplier detail, rank and outlier flags. Drag the handle.

slides.title: Scenario comparison, rebuilt around the comparison itself

bullets.text: Scenario setup reduced to a starting point rather than a blank form.
Bids, suppliers and criteria in one place for the first time.
The system points at what deserves attention.

slides.notes: Three to eight suppliers, ten-plus criteria. That is a matrix a person cannot hold in their head, which is why they were leaving.

slides.title: Navi gives the recommendation and the evidence, side by side
slides.standfirst: Cost-savings insights surfaced next to the underlying supplier data — so a user can accept the recommendation or audit it, in the same view.

bullets.text: The insight never appears without the data it was drawn from.
Placed inside the comparison workflow, not in a separate assistant panel.
Designed to be overruled: the recommendation is an input, not a decision.

items.alt: Navi AI assistant inside the scenario comparison workflow
items.label: Navi in context

slides.notes: Recommendation-plus-evidence is the pattern that survived testing. Recommendation alone tested badly in procurement, where being wrong is expensive and auditable.

slides.title: Material UI, extended where procurement needed something that did not exist
slides.standfirst: Timeline configurator, section markers, table actions, qualification panels — plus design tokens aligned with engineering so handoff was a lookup, not a negotiation.

figure.caption: 98+ screens are only maintainable as a system

slides.notes: Custom components were the exception and each one had to justify itself. Extending a foundation is cheaper than owning one.

pivot.detail: Usability testing showed users consistently missed modal-based contracts. The interaction model was already partly built; it moved to inline drill-down anyway.

slides.title: What it added up to

items.label: Screens on a reusable enterprise component system
Workflow stages designed as one system
Iterations validated in testing and stakeholder review
User-reported pain point eliminated: scenario navigation
Decision points mapped across the journey
Engineering teams aligned, with less rework at handoff

slides.notes: The number one pain point is the headline. It was the top user complaint before, and it is the thing twelve iterations were spent on.

slides.title: The easy architecture is a claim about how people work
slides.standfirst: A wizard is not a neutral container. Choosing it asserts that the task is sequential, and asserting that about procurement would have shipped the abandonment problem into a new interface.
slides.notes: This is the transferable point for a general audience. The specific product matters less than the habit of treating layout choices as empirical claims.

slides.title: Defend the harder architecture with evidence, and pivot when the evidence turns

bullets.text: Modals to inline, late and at cost

slides.notes: Expect the wizard question. Have the card-sort result ready, and be willing to say what would have changed your mind.
